title: Kahana vs WordPress: When the Cadence Needs a Shelf

columns.label: Ebook
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily get and consume ebooks on the platform (free or paid) as a first-class product, open, buy, borrow, or read without hunting.

columns.label: Short-form video
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily consume short-form video as a first-class surface (For You, Reels, Shorts).

columns.label: Long-form video
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily watch creator / UGC long-form video (or specialty long video) as a core surface. Course lectures belong under Courses. Hollywood catalogs belong under Series/Films.

columns.label: Series/Films
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily watch series and films as an SVOD / catalog entertainment product.

columns.label: Courses
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily take or browse structured courses as a first-class product.

columns.label: Newsletters
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily read or subscribe to newsletters / creator writing as a first-class product.

columns.label: Audio
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily listen to music, podcasts, or audiobooks as a first-class product.

columns.label: Memberships
columns.definition: Yes if a creator or seller can accept payments from others and make money through the platform, checkout, fan subscriptions, tips, ads, shop, or creator funds. Not only a classic Patreon-style membership product.

columns.label: Community & Messaging
columns.definition: Yes if you can create or join a group, community, or club, including group chats, Groups, subreddits, community tabs, discussion boards, or community feeds. A one-off comment on a single video or listing is not the bar; a durable place for the group to talk is.

columns.label: Storefronts
columns.definition: Yes if the product gives a creator a custom storefront or site that can take the place of building their own website (bio page, creator site, branded shop). Not a shop tab on someone else’s multi-seller marketplace.

columns.label: Marketplaces
columns.definition: Yes if a typical person can search and shop a catalog of offerings from many sellers, courses, books, digital goods, etc. Storefront software (Shopify, WooCommerce) is not a marketplace unless shoppers browse many sellers there.

scaleFacts: As of Jan 2026, WordPress powers ≈43–44% of all websites globally; with ~1.3–1.4B total websites that’s 590M+ active WordPress sites.
~409M people view over 20B pages each month through WordPress sites.
Tens of thousands of themes and 60k+ plugins enable blogs, portfolios, ecommerce, memberships, newsletters, and communities.
Core software is free (GPL); WordPress.com plans start at a few USD/month; managed hosting via third parties.

strengths.title: Mass adoption and ecosystem depth
strengths.detail: Dominant CMS with a huge plugin/theme ecosystem, newsletter, membership, commerce, LMS, and more can be added.

strengths.title: Flexible for many content types
strengths.detail: Blogs, media sites, newsletters, podcasts, portfolios, and content hubs with custom post types and taxonomies.

strengths.title: Ownership and portability
strengths.detail: Self-hosted WordPress gives full control over data, backups, and customization, easier to move hosts than closed platforms.

strengths.title: Huge community and tooling
strengths.detail: Vast docs, tutorials, agencies, and plugin vendors, easy to find help and third-party tools.

weaknesses.title: Maintenance and security overhead
weaknesses.detail: Core, themes, and plugins need updates; poorly managed sites can be vulnerable.

weaknesses.title: Complexity for non-technical users
weaknesses.detail: Plugin selection, performance, and styling can overwhelm vs more opinionated SaaS platforms.

weaknesses.title: Fragmented UX vs integrated SaaS
weaknesses.detail: Piecing together plugins/themes can create inconsistent UX and compatibility issues.

content:
Kahana is a library of curated hubs, Explore, Clubs, and optional Stripe. WordPress is writing, email, and subscriber publishing. They overlap in places and diverge in others.

What each one is

Kahana is built around hubs people can open, Explore so strangers can find them, Aura as scarce daily recognition, and Clubs so discussion outlives a feed. Selling stays optional.

WordPress is a free, open-source content management system that powers websites and blogs worldwide, enabling anyone to publish content, run newsletters, and extend functionality with themes and plugins.

Why this comparison

This article puts Kahana and WordPress side by side. It covers what each supports as a first-class product job, key features, and a few research notes so you have a clearer picture of what they are, how they compare, and what you can actually do on each one. It is not a teardown, and it is not a switch-tomorrow pitch.
contentAfter:
What you can do on each

On Kahana you can publish a hub, list it on Explore, discuss it in a Club, grant Aura, and turn on a Stripe paywall when you are ready to charge.

On WordPress you can use Newsletters, Memberships, and Storefronts as first-class product jobs. The inbox is the product: essays, archives, and paid subscriptions you already send on a cadence.

Using Kahana with WordPress

You can use both. WordPress keeps doing what it already does well. Kahana is another place to package the work, get discovered, and grow an audience.

Keep WordPress as distribution. Link a Kahana hub or Club as the deep destination: archives, files, and discussion that survive a missed email.
